name: Elena Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing law in Exeter. My week is lectures and tutorials, a few hours in the library every afternoon, and choir practice on Thursdays at the church near my flat. On Fridays I take the train home to Taunton, where I help out at my family's law office on Saturday mornings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the family law office.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's called Ito and Marsh, and my grandfather started it forty years ago. There are two solicitors, my mum and Mr. Marsh's daughter, plus three staff, and they do wills, house sales and family matters for people in town. I've always planned to join one day. My parents pay my fees and rent, so I have no debt, and I try not to waste that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's reassuring. I'd tell my choir friends it's another gadget, like the fax or the email, and the office will use it where it helps. I wouldn't say much online, because I don't think people want my opinion on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a little uneasy. Small town practices already struggle to attract young solicitors, and bigger firms with cheap software are taking the simple work. Even the mild version means less income for house sales and wills. The office isn't a goldmine to begin with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my degree and keep working Saturdays at the office. I'd ask my mum if she'd like me to look at the case-management software, since it's always breaking. I'd also look for a vacation scheme at a mid-size firm to see how bigger offices work, and I'd keep singing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own studies are fine, but the family office feels fragile, and I'm already carrying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by fragile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What do you mean by fragile? Two solicitors, three staff, and a lease in the high street that goes up each year. My mum works late and always says the business is one bad year away from trouble. I don't think she's exaggerating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help the office most in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would help the office most in this picture? A steady stream of clients, honestly, not technology. If more people made wills and sold homes, we'd be fine. I'd work on getting the office known to students and young families. My mum says the office is one bad year away from trouble, and I don't think she is exaggerating.

say: I'd tell choir friends it's **another gadget**, like fax or email.
I'd say little online, because people don't want my opinion on it.
think: Small town practices already struggle, and cheap software takes the **simple work**.
The office is **fragile**: two solicitors, three staff and a rising lease.
do: Keep **Saturdays** at the office and look at its case-management software.
Do a **vacation scheme** at a mid-size firm.
feel: **Uneasy**: her studies are fine, but the family office feels fragile.
S0.quote: My mum says the office is one bad year away from trouble, and I don't think she is exaggerating.
fieldNote: Elena's unease is about the **family office's money**, not about her own studies.
She is realistic that more local clients would help more than any technology.

steps.text: Keep working Saturdays at the family office in Taunton
Look at the office's case-management software with my mum
Do a vacation scheme at a mid-size firm to see how it works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's no surprise that change is coming. I'd tell my family at Sunday lunch that we should talk about the office and not wait. I'd say to the law society that small practices need training, not just big firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. Wills, conveyancing, which is the legal side of house sales, and standard letters are what the office does most of. If software does those, clients may go to cheaper online firms. I'd expect our income to fall within a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring it up with my mum, and I'd ask to sit in on the office's work so I can see what's routine. I'd try the tools once others have shown they work, and I'd learn to use one for drafting. I'd also focus on parts of law that need a person, like family and probate disputes, and keep my grades up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can't just be an observer, because it's my family. My mum's job, and one day mine, are tied to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the office do that software couldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does the office do that software couldn't? Sit across from a widow and explain what's happening, slowly, in plain words. A lot of our clients are old and don't like online forms. That's the thing I'd lean on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for helping small practices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for helping small practices? The law society, definitely, and the government, who've let the sector be squeezed for years. I'd like them to give small offices a small grant to modernise. A lot of our clients are old and don't like online forms, so sitting across from a widow and explaining is what we can offer.

say: I'd tell my family we should **talk about the office** and not wait.
I'd say small practices need **training**, not just big firms.
think: Wills, conveyancing and **standard letters** are most of the office's work.
Clients may go to **cheaper online** firms, so income could fall.
do: Sit in on the office's **routine work** and learn one drafting tool.
Focus on **family and probate** work that needs a person.
feel: **Anxious**: it is her family, and her mother's job and her own future are tied to it.
S1.quote: A lot of our clients are old and don't like online forms, so sitting across from a widow and explaining is what we can offer.
fieldNote: Elena is **anxious** because the card describes the family practice's core work almost exactly.
She sees real strength in the office's human, patient service to older clients.

steps.text: Sit in on the office's routine work to see what software could take
Learn one drafting tool once others have shown it works
Focus on family and probate disputes that need a person
Ask the law society about grants for small practices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for every institution to wake up, and that small towns must not be forgotten. I'd tell my family we need a plan for the office. I'd also write to my MP, who has a surgery in Taunton on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. The office is built on routine legal work, and in two years that's the first thing to go. I'd graduate in 2029, a year after, with no office to go back to. I'd be worrying about my mum's income and the three staff who depend on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my mum about options: sell the practice while it has value, merge with a bigger firm, or change to advice and disputes. I'd keep my degree going, but I'd also look at work with people, like mediation. I'd save everything I could and ask my parents to keep their savings safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the whole structure of what I thought my future was. I'd lie awake thinking about Mr. Marsh's daughter and the staff, and what happens to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years do compared with the longer ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does two years do compared with the longer ones? It takes away the chance to hand the office over slowly. Normally mum would retire in ten years and I'd take over. Here there might be no office to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in those two years? A guarantee for small firms like ours: help with closing or changing without losing everything. And proper income support for staff, so a receptionist isn't left with nothing. Normally my mum would retire in ten years and I'd take over, but in two years there might be no office left to take.

say: I'd say every institution must **wake up** and small towns must not be forgotten.
I'd write to my **MP** at her Friday surgery.
think: The office is built on **routine work**, which goes first in two years.
I'd graduate in 2029 with **no office** to go back to.
do: Ask my mum whether to **sell, merge** or move to advice and disputes.
**Save** everything I can and consider mediation work.
feel: **Alarmed**: the whole structure of her future, and she'd lie awake over the staff.
S2.quote: Normally my mum would retire in ten years and I'd take over, but in two years there might be no office left to take.
fieldNote: Elena is **alarmed** because the family office's survival and her whole plan rest on the work that goes first.
Her worry extends to named colleagues: Mr. Marsh's daughter and three staff.

steps.text: Ask my mum whether to sell, merge or switch to disputes and advice
Save everything I can from the family allowance
Write to my MP at her Taunton Friday surgery about small firms
Ask the law society and council for help for small practices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but it's enough to organise. I'd tell my mum and the law society that small practices should prepare together, with shared training and shared systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious but I'd feel there's a chance. I'd graduate in 2029, and the office would have two years to adapt before 2031. If we move to advice, disputes and care for older clients, we could survive, or at least be sold in good shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and spend each summer at the office, redesigning it with my mum. I'd learn the tools properly once they're proven, and I'd try one new service, like online wills for old clients with a visit from a person. I'd save, and keep my choir and church life as an anchor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel a bit more in control, because five years gives me something to do, and I like being useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How is five years different from the two-year picture? In two years I'm watching it happen. In five I could be part of the fix. It's about whether I'm helpless or useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the other solicitor at the office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell Mr. Marsh's daughter, the other solicitor? To start looking now at what services clients need that a screen can't give. Not to wait until the clients start leaving. In two years I'd be watching it happen, but in five years I could be part of the fix.

say: I'd say five years is **short but enough** to organise.
I'd tell my mum small practices should **prepare together**.
think: The office would have **two years** to adapt before 2031.
If we move to advice and care for older clients, we could **survive**.
do: Spend summers **redesigning the office** with my mum.
Try one **new service**, such as online wills with a person's visit.
feel: **Anxious**, but more in control, because she has something useful to do.
S3.quote: In two years I'd be watching it happen, but in five years I could be part of the fix.
fieldNote: Elena's steady style shows: she wants to be **useful**, moving from helpless in two years to part of the fix in five.
Her plan is the family firm's survival, not her own escape.

steps.text: Spend each summer redesigning the family office with my mum
Try a new service combining online wills with a home visit
Learn the AI tools properly once they are proven
Save part of my allowance each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and we should treat it as a gift. I'd tell small practices to share ideas and train their staff slowly. I'd say it at church and with my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly settled. By 2036 I'd be 28, qualified, and probably already in the family office. We'd have changed it step by step, with services people still want. The robots wouldn't come until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and train at a firm for a couple of years. Then I'd join my mum and change the office gradually: more advice and family law, and tools for the dull parts. I'd also keep saving, and I'd marry, maybe, and have a family of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. I'd carry the same worry as any family business, but with time to do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong during the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What could still go wrong in the ten years? Clients might leave before we adapt. If a cheap online service gets popular in year three, we'd lose a lot of wills and house sales, and I'd have to decide whether to adapt or sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if it went that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do if it went that way? I'd talk to mum and say we should sell while the practice still has value, and I'd work for another firm. It wouldn't be a tragedy, just a change. If a cheap online will service gets popular in year three, I'd have to decide whether the family office adapts or sells.

say: I'd say ten years is **a gift**, and small practices should share ideas.
I'd say it at church and to my mum.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28 and **in the family office**, which we'd have changed step by step.
Robots wouldn't reach hands-on work until **2039**.
do: Train at a firm for **two years**, then join my mum and change the office.
**Save** steadily in case the office must be sold.
feel: **Uneasy** only a little, like any family business but with time to act.
S4.quote: If a cheap online will service gets popular in year three, I'd have to decide whether the family office adapts or sells.
fieldNote: Elena's mood is **uneasy**, because the family office's fate stays open even with ten years.
She has a realistic exit: sell while it has value, and treat it as change, not tragedy.

steps.text: Train at a mid-size firm for two years after graduating
Join my mum and shift the office to advice and family law
Keep saving in case the office has to be sold

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because the office does mostly wills and house sales, and those are exactly the routine work a machine could take. What would help is time, and rules that stop big firms from taking small town practices' clients overnight. Also advice from the law society about what a small office should do first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not against new things, I only want them proven. I'd be happier if people said what small offices like ours can do, instead of talking only about the big firms in London. My family's law office does wills and house sales for the whole town, and I can't tell if that is a safe job or a target.

headlineQuote: My family's law office does wills and house sales for the whole town, and I can't tell if that is a safe job or a target.
portrait: **Elena** is an 18-year-old law student in Exeter whose family runs a small solicitors' office in Taunton.
She sings in a **church choir**, plans to join the family practice, and holds traditional views on faith, work and community.
She uses AI tools **now and then**, once others have shown they work, and is steady rather than fast.
The family office does **routine work** like wills and house sales, so her mood is worried even in mild worlds.
She wants **time and clear advice** for small practices, and fears big firms taking their clients.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028**, because the family office does routine wills and house sales.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **time and rules** that protect small town practices, plus clear advice from the law society.
